decisions.decision: Data & Training Pipeline: Determining how much effort allows us to ship.
decisions.answer: R1: Evidence does not say massive data is non-negotiable; it highlights quality and specialized scope. Small, high-quality instruction datasets are portrayed as high leverage but not explicitly sufficient alone, so necessity of massive data is not established.
decisions.notes: Video section stresses that high-quality annotations are urgent and noisy labels hurt performance, but does not claim that only massive datasets work. Audio section credits “large-scale datasets for instruction fine-tuning” for advances, implying scale helps but not that it is strictly required. MiniGPT-4 and InstructBLIP descriptions emphasize two-stage pipelines with a smaller, high-quality fine-tuning stage, supporting the idea that high-quality instruction data is especially valuable. The big-vs-small debate suggests specialized models can perform well without necessarily requiring massive general-purpose data. However, nowhere is it stated that a small dataset alone is enough, so we cannot be stronger than this nuanced answer.

decisions.decision: Data & Training Pipeline: Determining how much effort allows us to ship.
decisions.answer: R2: The survey clearly presents two-stage pipelines that fine-tune pre-trained models (frozen encoders/LLMs plus adapters) as a viable and commonly used path; it does not require pre-training from scratch.
decisions.notes: MiniGPT-4 keeps the pre-trained vision encoder and LLM frozen and trains only a projection layer, then a short fine-tune, which is a textbook two-stage pipeline. InstructBLIP initializes from BLIP-2 checkpoints and tunes only Q-Former and then instruction-tunes, again reusing pre-trained components. NeXT-GPT uses ImageBind and Vicuna 7B with projection layers, another example of building on pre-trained backbones. This all supports that fine-tuning pre-trained models is a standard, viable approach; no evidence suggests pre-training from scratch is mandatory.
